quote_item6: In this study, misinformation is defined as any false, inaccurate, or conspiratorial information pertaining to COVID-19 and vaccination. ... Our annotation training adhered to the COVID-19 misinformation codebook by Memon and Carley (2020), a model for subsequent studies (Moffitt et al., 2021).
quote_item10: Similarly, the misinformation classification model identifies 460,087 tweets as misinformation, accounting for over 27% of the dataset.
notes: Item 6 LOW: external pre-existing published codebook (Memon & Carley 2020) plus consultation of fact-checking sites = external anchor. Items 1-2 HIGH: universe is a 147-keyword Finnish vaccine-tweet corpus, not an audience; authors concede Twitter's 'lack of representativeness of the general population'. Item 3 LOW: full census of the keyword frame. Item 7 HIGH: misinformation classifier F1 = 0.67 (accuracy 0.85) and the classifier-labelled rate (27%) is ~1.6x the human-annotated rate in the training sample (709/4150 = 17%), so the instrument is not shown valid at the prevalence claim it supports; Krippendorff's alpha 0.668 is only 'good' by the authors' own cut-offs. Item 9 LOW: Dec 2019-Oct 2022 stated. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is a topical keyword corpus, reported as 'Approximately a third of tweets contained misinformation'.

quote_item6: I, therefore, use misinformation as an umbrella term, following Sanaullah et al. [19], defining it as any information that is incorrect, misleading, or false, regardless of the intent of the disseminator.
quote_item10: This results in a final dataset of 426,262 binary classified tweets, with a proportion of 5.11% being classified as containing misinformation.
notes: Item 6 HIGH: adopting another paper's CONCEPTUAL definition is not an external ground truth; operationalisation is an author-written codebook (Appendix 1) applied to 994 tweets with no fact-check verdicts, credibility list or external verification behind it - internal and ad hoc under the ruling. Items 1-2 HIGH: Norwegian COVID-keyword tweet corpus, not an audience. Item 3 LOW: census of the keyword frame. Item 7 LOW: kappa 0.78 between two annotators, third-annotator adjudication, plus a blind 300-tweet validation of the classifier (kappa 0.791). Item 10 HIGH: topical keyword denominator; the CONCENTRATION estimate (25% of users = 75% of misinfo) has a denominator restricted to misinformation-posting users. Both 6 and 10 HIGH -> overall HIGH. Note the self-training pipeline dumps 130,065 unpredictable tweets into the non-misinformation class, a stated false-negative risk.

quote_item6: This study employed two data sources: subtitles from ten German public broadcast news or talk shows between June 2023 and June 2024 (n = 1382) and checked claims in articles from six German fact-checking organizations between January 2023 and June 2024 (n = 462).
quote_item10: It finds 77 matches in 67 episodes, amounting to 4.85% of the 1382 episodes during the sampling period between June 2023 and June 2024.
notes: Strongest study in this shard. Item 6 LOW: case definition is external fact-check verdicts from six German organisations (four of them IFCN signatories, three in Meta's 3PFC). Items 1-3 LOW: near-census of all 1382 episodes of the ten most-watched German public-broadcast news and talk shows over 12 months - a real, large audience, no selection on the outcome. Items 4-5 NA (content analysis of broadcast supply). Item 7 LOW: retrieval pipeline validated (ChatGPT matching F1 = 84.21%; false-negative rate estimated at 14% against a hand-built benchmark) with three student annotators validating candidate pairs; the single-expert step covers descriptive categories (speaker, deception type), not the prevalence numerator. Item 10 LOW: denominator is the full episode population, not a curated subset. Caveat recorded, not scored: the numerator is a lower bound because only claims a fact-checker had already checked can match - the author states 'This biased selection renders the study exploratory in nature rather than representative.'

quote_item6: To evaluate the presence of incorrect information, the content was analysed by comparing the claims made with information on PubMed, in medical literature, or other reliable sources like medical journals.
quote_item10: Sixty-eight percent of 121 posts did not present any misinformation. Thirty-two percent of videos contained some form of medically related misinformation.
notes: Item 6 LOW: falsity anchored to external, pre-existing peer-reviewed medical evidence (PubMed / medical journals) rather than author opinion - the 'expert-verified false claims' route; the DISCERN-style quality-instrument failure mode does not apply here. Items 1-3 HIGH: 25 hashtags searched then 'filtered for the highest number of Likes' - a popularity-filtered, topic-curated corpus of only 121 videos; authors concede 'our findings may include selection bias'. Item 7 HIGH: 'The reliability of our findings may be reduced because of the initial classification of misinformation by one coder.' No kappa, no validated instrument. Item 9 UNCLEAR: no data-collection date or observation window is stated anywhere in the paper (treated as HIGH in the overall per the instrument, recorded separately here). Item 10 HIGH: 121 popularity-filtered hashtag videos as denominator for a headline 32% figure. n_high = 5 affirmative HIGH; overall HIGH because item 9 UNCLEAR counts as HIGH in the summary judgement (6).

quote_item6: Following best practice for source-based research on misinformation and news trustworthiness (Lin et al., 2023; Luhring et al., 2024), we used NewsGuard-an established database for source-based news credibility labels rated according to apolitical journalistic standards-to classify websites as trustworthy or untrustworthy. ... Sources are considered untrustworthy if the score is below 60 on a 0-100 scale.
quote_item10: We focus on two individual-level measures of exposure: the share of visits to untrustworthy news outlets among all news visits-in the raw data 0.75% in 2017 and 0.52% in 2024-and the average NewsGuard score (ranging from 0-lowest to 100-highest reliability) across all news visits, in the raw data, stable at 96 in both years.
notes: Item 6 LOW: NewsGuard is a published source-level credibility list - LOW on its own merits and squarely inside the 2026-07-23 ruling. Items 1-3 LOW: German adults from the YouGov Pulse panel, 2017 wave quota-matched to the online population and matching the actual AfD vote share (13.9% vs 12.6%); complete passive behavioural trace (56M URL visits) rather than a sample of visits. Item 4 LOW: opt-in/coverage bias explicitly addressed - the 2024 wave's AfD underrepresentation is quantified against the 2025 election and the authors state their 'estimates likely understate actual levels of exposure'; response/attrition rates themselves are not reported. Item 5 LOW: passive metering of the subjects' own browsing. Item 7 LOW: NewsGuard validated externally (Lin et al. 2023 correspondence across rating sets) and results robust to score thresholds of 50 and 70. Item 8 LOW: 2017 desktop-only vs 2024 desktop+mobile, but a desktop-only robustness specification is run. Item 9 LOW: 6-month (2017) and 2-month (2024) windows stated, and the authors explicitly flag that the binary reach indicator is window-sensitive. Item 10 LOW: denominators are all news visits and all participants - a real audience's whole news diet. Only the two CONCENTRATION estimates use a within-untrustworthy denominator, which is correct for a concentration measure.

quote_item6: Potential claims were then independently reviewed by two subject matter experts, both cardiology fellows, and classified as true or false. Claims that were partially true, misleading, or lacking important clinical context were classified as false for the purposes of analysis.
quote_item10: Of 1,349 screened videos, 258 met inclusion criteria. ... False claims were identified in 39.5% of videos.
notes: Item 6 LOW: expert-verified false claims adjudicated by two cardiology fellows against peer-reviewed evidence with consensus resolution = external anchor. The DISCERN/GQS/PEMAT-AV instruments are used for a SEPARATE quality analysis and do not stand in for falsity, so the quality-instrument exclusion is not triggered. Items 1-2 HIGH: search-term-seeded statin corpus, not an audience. Item 3 LOW: full scrape of the search results (1,349 unique videos) with dual independent eligibility screening, not top-N by engagement. Item 7 HIGH: the reported ICCs (0.808-0.906) are for the QUALITY scales only; no reliability statistic and no validated instrument for the false-claim variable that produces the 39.5%. Item 9 HIGH: single-day cross-sectional scrape ('Data was collected on November 14, 2025') with no stated posting-date range, generalised to prevalence. Item 10 HIGH: denominator is 258 inclusion-filtered statin videos, and the false-claim category breakdown uses total false claims as its denominator. 5 affirmative HIGH with item 6 LOW -> MODERATE. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

quote_item6: For this context, sunscreen misinformation was defined as when TikTok content critiqued sunscreen for either having harmful effects on one's body or conversely preventing the benefits of sun exposure, which included ideas that sunscreen is unnecessary or ineffective. ... Sunscreen misinformation was thus defined from a public health perspective where TikToks, in one form or another, dissuaded its use to the detriment of its valuable health benefits.
quote_item10: We conducted a content analysis on 971 of the most viewed TikTok videos across the five most popular and relevant sunscreen-related hashtags (#sunscreen, #sunscreenviral, #spf, #sunscreenreview, #sunprotection).
notes: Item 6 HIGH: the case definition is a project-specific, iteratively developed coding frame built from the authors' own 'public health perspective' - critique-of-sunscreen as a proxy for falsity, with no fact-check verdicts, credibility list or independent expert adjudication; the authors explicitly did not verify individual product claims ('Analysis was not conducted on each individual product profiled to determine whether a product with low SPF was inaccurately promoted'). Internal and ad hoc under the ruling. Items 1-3 HIGH: five hashtags, 5,040 scraped, then the 3,040 least-viewed removed and one video kept per account - top-N-by-views on a topic-curated frame. Item 7 HIGH: two coders with audits and consensus but no kappa or any reliability statistic, and the coding frame is unvalidated. Item 9 HIGH: hashtag census taken Sept 26 / Oct 4 2024, but no observation window is defined for the video corpus itself, which spans arbitrary upload dates. Item 10 HIGH: 971 most-viewed hashtag videos as the denominator for a claim about how prevalent sunscreen misinformation is. Both 6 and 10 HIGH and 7 affirmative HIGH -> overall HIGH. Note the estimate is LOW (6.0%), so this is a case where high risk of bias does not co-occur with a high number.
